drivingInfo: Mauritius drives on the left-hand side of the road, similar to the UK, Australia and India. Roads are generally well-maintained and signposted.
The island is compact — most destinations are reachable within 1–2 hours from anywhere. A rental car is the perfect way to explore at your own pace.
You will need a valid driving licence from your home country. Most international licences are accepted.
The minimum driving age in Mauritius is 18 years. Renters must be 21 or over.

paragliding.pageDescription: Soar above Mauritius on a tandem paragliding adventure with MauTravel. Four spectacular flying locations — Le Morne, Chamarel, Montagne Longue & Quatre Sœurs. From €170 per person. Certified professional pilots.
paragliding.heroSubtitle: Experience Mauritius from an entirely new perspective as you soar above mountains, lagoons, and breathtaking landscapes with a certified tandem paragliding pilot.
about: MauTravel's tandem paragliding experience offers one of the most extraordinary perspectives of Mauritius — drifting freely above volcanic peaks, forested valleys, and the endless turquoise expanse of the Indian Ocean. With four exceptional flying sites across the island, each flight reveals a different and equally breathtaking side of Mauritius that simply cannot be appreciated from the ground.

From the dramatic central highlands of Montagne Longue and the east-coast splendour of Quatre Sœurs, to the forested ridges of Chamarel and the iconic lagoon of Le Morne — every location offers its own unique landscape and atmosphere. Your pilot selects the ideal take-off site on the day based on prevailing wind and weather conditions, ensuring the finest views and the safest possible flight for every guest.

Tandem paragliding is entirely suitable for beginners — no previous experience is required. You are secured alongside a fully certified, experienced professional pilot throughout the entire flight, from take-off to landing. All flights begin with a thorough safety briefing and equipment check. Advance booking is strongly recommended to confirm your preferred date and receive personalised assistance from our team.

locations.name: Montagne Longue
locations.subtitle: Central Highlands Flying
locations.description: Set within the central highlands of Mauritius, Montagne Longue offers an authentic inland mountain paragliding experience unlike any other on the island. A gentle 20-minute ascent to the take-off point rewards you with sweeping panoramas across volcanic ridges and lush green valleys stretching in every direction.
landmarks: Potential extension toward Pieter Both (weather permitting)

locations.name: Quatre Sœurs
locations.subtitle: East Coast Adventure
locations.description: Perched on the east coast of Mauritius, Quatre Sœurs delivers a spectacular combination of mountain grandeur and ocean panoramas. A 20–30-minute ascent to the launch site reveals breathtaking views across verdant valleys, rugged ridges, and the shimmering Indian Ocean coastline stretching to the horizon.
landmarks: Views toward Les Chats et la Souris and Montagne Bambous
Sweeping valleys and mountain ridge scenery

locations.name: Chamarel
locations.subtitle: Rugged Valley Scenery
locations.description: Chamarel's rugged and richly forested landscape provides a stunning natural amphitheatre for paragliding. Just a 10-minute walk from the launch area, pilots and passengers take flight from one of Mauritius's most scenic regions — with forested mountain ridges gradually opening toward the sparkling west coast and the vast Indian Ocean beyond.
landmarks: Gradual reveal of the west coast and Indian Ocean

locations.name: Le Morne
locations.subtitle: Mauritius's Most Iconic Flight
locations.description: Le Morne is widely regarded as the most celebrated paragliding destination on the island. The 30-minute ascent to the take-off site culminates in one of Mauritius's most spectacular launches — with the legendary turquoise Le Morne lagoon spread out below, and the world-famous underwater waterfall illusion often visible from above on clear days.
landmarks: Breathtaking Le Morne lagoon and peninsula views
The iconic underwater waterfall illusion (visible from above)
Turquoise lagoon meeting the open Indian Ocean

included: Take-off location selected for best conditions
notIncluded: Hotel transfers (available on request — please enquire)
Gratuities for your pilot (entirely at your discretion)

paragliding.activityReviewsNote: These reviews are from guests who experienced tandem paragliding with one of MauTravel's trusted local activity partners.

faqs.question: Do I need previous paragliding experience?
faqs.answer: No experience is required at all. Tandem paragliding means you fly secured in a harness alongside a certified professional pilot who manages every aspect of the flight — from launch to landing. Your only role is to relax, enjoy the views, and take it all in.

faqs.question: Is tandem paragliding safe?
faqs.answer: Tandem paragliding with MauTravel is conducted exclusively with fully certified, experienced professional pilots using regularly inspected and approved safety equipment. All flights are weather-dependent and will only proceed when conditions are assessed as safe by your pilot. Your safety is the absolute priority at every step.

faqs.question: What should I wear and bring?
faqs.answer: Wear comfortable, close-fitting clothing appropriate for the weather. Sturdy closed-toe shoes — trainers or walking shoes — are strongly recommended. Avoid scarves, loose layers, or flowing garments. Sunglasses with a secure strap and sunscreen are advisable. Your pilot will provide any additional pre-flight guidance.

faqs.question: Can children participate?
faqs.answer: Children may participate subject to minimum age, weight, and health requirements. We recommend contacting MauTravel directly via WhatsApp with your child's age and weight before booking so we can confirm eligibility and advise accordingly.

faqs.question: How long is the total paragliding experience?
faqs.answer: The complete experience — including the ascent to the take-off site, equipment fitting, safety briefing, and the flight itself — typically takes between 45 minutes and 2 hours depending on the location chosen. The actual paragliding flight lasts approximately 15–25 minutes.

faqs.question: What happens if the weather is unsuitable on my booking date?
faqs.answer: Your pilot and the MauTravel team monitor wind and weather conditions carefully ahead of every flight. If conditions are not suitable on your scheduled date, we will contact you promptly to reschedule to the next available date at no additional charge.

faqs.question: Can I take my phone or camera during the flight?
faqs.answer: We strongly recommend securing all personal belongings before take-off. Phones and cameras must be attached with a wrist strap or mounted on a secure harness. Your pilot will advise on what is safe to carry. A professional photo and video package may be available on request — please enquire when booking.

hiking-adventures.name: Hiking Adventures
hiking-adventures.pageTitle: Hiking in Mauritius — Guided Mountain & Trail Hikes
hiking-adventures.pageDescription: Explore Mauritius's volcanic peaks and forest trails on expert-guided hikes. Le Morne, Pieter Both, Le Pouce, Lion Mountain and more. Book with MauTravel.
hiking-adventures.heroSubtitle: Conquer volcanic summits, traverse forested ridges, and discover sweeping panoramas of the Mauritian landscape on guided hikes suited to every level — from gentle walks to challenging peak ascents.
about: Mauritius is far more than beaches — its volcanic interior is laced with dramatic mountain trails, dense forests, and viewpoints that reward the effort with unforgettable panoramas of turquoise lagoons and rolling sugarcane fields. MauTravel partners with expert local guides who know every trail intimately.

Our hiking programme covers the full range of Mauritius's peaks and trails: the iconic UNESCO-listed Le Morne Brabant, the challenging rock scramble of Pieter Both, the accessible ridgeline of Le Pouce above Port Louis, and lesser-known gems like Piton Savanne, Tourelle du Tamarin and Montagne Cocotte. Each hike is tailored to your group's fitness level and interests.

All hikes are led by certified, experienced guides who provide full equipment guidance, safety briefings, and fascinating insights into the island's geology, flora and fauna. Whether you're a first-time hiker or a seasoned trail runner, we have a route that will challenge and inspire you.
notIncluded: Hiking boots (strongly recommended — rental available on request)
National park entry fees where applicable

pricing.name: Half Day Hike
pricing.description: A 3–4 hour guided hike on one of our shorter routes such as Le Pouce or Corps de Garde.

pricing.name: Full Day Hike
pricing.description: A 6–8 hour guided ascent of a major peak — Le Morne, Pieter Both or Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire.

pricing.name: Private Group Package
pricing.description: Exclusive guided hiking for your group — choose your peak and we build a custom day around your abilities.

faqs.question: Do I need prior hiking experience?
faqs.answer: Not at all. We offer routes graded from beginner-friendly (Le Pouce, Signal Mountain) to challenging technical ascents (Pieter Both, Piton de la Petite Rivière Noire). Tell us your fitness level when booking and we'll match you to the perfect trail.

faqs.question: What should I wear and bring?
faqs.answer: We recommend lightweight, breathable clothing, sturdy closed-toe shoes or hiking boots, a hat, sunscreen, and a small daypack. We provide water but suggest bringing extra snacks. A full kit list is sent upon booking confirmation.

faqs.question: Is Le Morne suitable for beginners?
faqs.answer: The lower section of Le Morne Brabant is accessible to reasonably fit beginners. The upper section involves some scrambling and is recommended for those comfortable with heights and uneven terrain. Your guide will advise on the day based on conditions and your group's ability.

faqs.question: What is the best time of year for hiking in Mauritius?
faqs.answer: The cooler, drier months of May to November are ideal for hiking. Trails can be slippery during the wet season (December to April) and some routes may be temporarily closed after heavy rain. We monitor conditions daily and will advise if a route needs to be adjusted.

faqs.question: How fit do I need to be for the full-day hikes?
faqs.answer: Full-day hikes to major peaks such as Pieter Both or Le Morne Brabant require a good level of fitness and comfortable walking for 5–7 hours. If you are unsure, start with a half-day hike to assess your stamina, or contact us to discuss your fitness level before booking.

waterfalls-river-treks.name: Waterfalls & River Treks
waterfalls-river-treks.pageDescription: Discover Mauritius's hidden waterfalls and jungle river treks — Tamarind Falls, Rochester Falls, 500ft Waterfall and more. Guided adventures with MauTravel.
waterfalls-river-treks.heroSubtitle: Follow wild rivers through tropical gorges, swim beneath thundering cascades, and discover the hidden natural wonders of Mauritius's lush interior — experiences that no beach excursion can match.
about: Mauritius hides some of the Indian Ocean's most spectacular waterfalls and river gorges deep within its volcanic interior. MauTravel's waterfall and river trek experiences take you off the tourist trail and into landscapes of extraordinary natural beauty — thick jungle canopy, volcanic rock formations, and crystal-clear freshwater pools.

The undisputed highlight of any waterfall itinerary is the Tamarind Falls — also known as the 7 Cascades — a series of seven magnificent waterfalls cascading through a steep, forested gorge in the Tamarin area. Other unmissable destinations include the dramatically flat ledge of Rochester Falls, the powerful 500ft Waterfall, the tranquil Alexandra Falls, and the serene Eau Bleue and Léon waterfalls tucked away in the island's southern highlands.

Every trek is led by experienced local guides who know the safest river crossings, the best swimming pools, and the hidden viewpoints that make each journey unique. These are genuine wilderness experiences — not tourist paths — so you can expect mud, water, and memories that last a lifetime.
notIncluded: Water shoes or trekking sandals (essential — rental available)
Change of clothing for after swimming

pricing.name: Single Waterfall Trek
pricing.description: A half-day guided trek to one major waterfall with swimming — perfect for families or those short on time.

pricing.name: Tamarind 7 Cascades
pricing.description: The signature waterfall experience — a full traverse of all seven cascades in the Tamarin gorge.

pricing.name: Multi-Waterfall Day
pricing.description: Visit two or three different waterfall sites in one day for the ultimate Mauritius waterfall experience.

faqs.question: How difficult are the river treks?
faqs.answer: Most waterfall treks are rated moderate — they involve walking on uneven terrain, crossing streams, and scrambling over rocks. Participants should be reasonably fit and comfortable on rough ground. We do not recommend these treks for guests with serious mobility issues.

faqs.question: What footwear should I wear?
faqs.answer: Water shoes or sturdy trekking sandals with grip are essential. Regular trainers are not suitable as they will get wet and can become slippery. If you don't have suitable footwear, please let us know and we can advise on rental options.

faqs.question: Is it safe to swim in the waterfalls?
faqs.answer: Yes — we only swim at locations that our guides have assessed as safe. We avoid swimming during or immediately after heavy rainfall when currents can be stronger. Your guide will assess conditions on the day and make the final decision on swimming.

faqs.question: Can children participate?
faqs.answer: Children aged 8 and above can join most waterfall treks with a parent or guardian. Some more challenging routes are adult-only. Please advise us of children's ages when booking so we can recommend the most suitable experience.

faqs.question: What is the best waterfall to visit in Mauritius?
faqs.answer: Tamarind Falls (7 Cascades) is widely considered the most spectacular and is our most popular trek. Rochester Falls is the easiest and most accessible, making it great for families. The 500ft Waterfall offers the most dramatic single cascade. We can recommend the best option for your group.

7-caves-exploration.name: 7 Caves Exploration
7-caves-exploration.pageTitle: 7 Caves Exploration Mauritius | Volcanic Lava Tube Adventure | MauTravel
7-caves-exploration.pageDescription: Discover the hidden volcanic lava tubes of Mauritius on a guided 7 Caves Exploration. Journey through ancient underground chambers, spectacular rock formations and geological wonders. Book with MauTravel.
7-caves-exploration.heroSubtitle: Journey beneath the surface and discover the hidden volcanic world of Mauritius — ancient lava tubes, dramatic underground chambers, and geological wonders that most visitors never see.
about: Beneath the lush surface of Mauritius lies a geological underworld of extraordinary beauty. Formed millions of years ago during periods of intense volcanic activity, the island's lava tubes are among its most remarkable and least-known natural treasures. The 7 Caves Exploration takes you deep into this hidden world — a series of interconnected volcanic tunnels and chambers that wind through ancient rock formations shaped by rivers of molten lava long before human eyes ever saw them.

Walking through these underground passages is a genuinely immersive experience. The cave walls reveal layer upon layer of volcanic history — smooth lava flows, dramatic stalactite formations, and rock textures in striking shades of black, red and ochre. Your expert local guide brings the geology to life, explaining how each chamber was formed and what it tells us about the volcanic origins of the island. It is a rare opportunity to understand Mauritius not just as a tropical paradise, but as a place of extraordinary geological significance.

The 7 Caves Exploration is designed to be accessible to a wide range of guests — no previous caving or climbing experience is required. The pace is relaxed and the route is carefully chosen to balance discovery with safety. Whether you are a curious family, a couple seeking something beyond the beach, or a dedicated nature lover, this underground adventure will be one of the most memorable and unexpected highlights of your time in Mauritius.
included: Expert local guide with geological knowledge

pricing.name: Guided Cave Exploration
pricing.description: A fully guided 3–4 hour exploration of all 7 volcanic caves with expert geological commentary.

pricing.name: Private Group Tour
pricing.description: An exclusive private exploration for your group — ideal for families, couples and small parties.

faqs.question: Is the cave exploration safe?
faqs.answer: Yes. The 7 Caves tour is fully guided by an experienced local expert and is suitable for beginners. A comprehensive safety briefing is given before entry, and helmets and head torches are provided. The route has been carefully selected to offer a genuine underground experience while maintaining the highest safety standards throughout.

faqs.question: Can children join the exploration?
faqs.answer: Yes, children aged 8 and above can participate with a parent or guardian. The route is accessible for reasonably active children and the pace is always set to suit the group. Please advise us of children's ages when booking so we can prepare accordingly and confirm the most suitable route.

faqs.question: Do I need previous caving experience?
faqs.answer: No previous experience is required at all. The 7 Caves Exploration is designed for first-time visitors to underground environments. Your guide will walk you through every step and the pace is entirely relaxed — there is no rushing, no climbing, and no tight passages that require special skills.

faqs.question: What should I wear?
faqs.answer: Comfortable, fitted clothing that you don't mind getting dusty is ideal. Closed-toe shoes with a good grip are essential — sandals, open shoes and flip-flops are not permitted for safety reasons. The temperature inside the caves is slightly cooler than outside, so a light layer is a good idea. Helmets are provided.

faqs.question: Is photography allowed inside the caves?
faqs.answer: Absolutely — photography is warmly encouraged. Smartphones and compact cameras work well inside the caves. Your guide will point out the best formations and lighting angles for memorable shots. Please take care not to touch or lean on geological formations when positioning for photographs.

faqs.question: What is the best time of day to visit?
faqs.answer: The caves can be explored in the morning or afternoon, and conditions inside remain consistent throughout the day regardless of external weather. Morning departures are popular for guests who wish to combine the cave exploration with another activity in the afternoon. We will confirm the ideal departure time when you book.

wild-south-experience.name: The Wild South Experience
wild-south-experience.pageTitle: Wild South Mauritius — Gris Gris, Natural Pools & Hidden Beaches
wild-south-experience.pageDescription: Explore the dramatic and untouched southern coast of Mauritius — Gris Gris cliffs, natural rock pools, hidden beaches and scenic viewpoints. Book with MauTravel.
wild-south-experience.heroSubtitle: Discover the wild, untouched southern coastline of Mauritius — volcanic cliffs, crashing ocean waves, secret rock pools, and hidden beaches that the resort crowds never find.
about: The south coast of Mauritius is a world apart from the calm lagoons and resort hotels that most visitors experience. Here, the Indian Ocean meets the island with full force — dramatic volcanic cliffs, powerful surf, and rugged coastal scenery that feels genuinely wild and untouched. The Wild South Experience is our signature full-day exploration of this extraordinary coastline.

The centrepiece is Gris Gris, arguably the most dramatic viewpoint on the entire island — a clifftop promontory where waves crash spectacularly against black volcanic rock while the ocean stretches uninterrupted to Antarctica. From here, the journey continues along the southern coast, discovering natural rock pools carved by centuries of wave action, secret beaches accessible only by foot, and sweeping panoramic viewpoints over the ocean and the highlands.

Unlike a standard island tour, the Wild South Experience is designed for guests who want to move beyond the postcard scenes and encounter Mauritius in its most raw, authentic form. Your guide brings deep local knowledge of every hidden path, viewpoint and pool along the route — places that simply aren't in any guidebook.

highlights.label: Highlights
highlights.value: Gris Gris, natural pools, hidden beaches

included: Packed lunch or lunch stop at local restaurant
notIncluded: Swimming costume and towel (for natural pools)

pricing.name: Wild South Day
pricing.description: A full-day private exploration of the southern coast with a knowledgeable local guide.

pricing.name: South & Highlands Combo
pricing.description: Combine the Wild South coastal route with the Black River Gorges highland scenery for a comprehensive southern day.

pricing.name: Photography Special
pricing.description: A photographer-focused version of the Wild South tour, timed for golden-hour light at Gris Gris and the coastal cliffs.

faqs.question: Is the Wild South suitable for families with young children?
faqs.answer: The Wild South Experience is best suited to adults and older children (10+) due to the uneven cliff-top terrain near Gris Gris and some of the natural pool locations. The vehicle-based sections are suitable for all ages. Please contact us to discuss your group composition.

faqs.question: Can we swim at the natural pools?
faqs.answer: Yes — the natural rock pools along the southern coast are sheltered enough for safe swimming on most days. However, the open coastline at Gris Gris is not suitable for swimming due to strong currents and waves. Your guide will always assess conditions before any water entry.

faqs.question: What is the road access like on the south coast?
faqs.answer: Most of the southern coastal route is accessed via good tar roads. Some hidden locations involve short walks on rough coastal tracks. Our vehicles are well-maintained and suitable for the terrain. We recommend wearing comfortable shoes for the walking sections.

faqs.question: Is this different from a standard South Tour?
faqs.answer: Yes, significantly. A standard South Tour typically focuses on popular stops like Chamarel Coloured Earths, Le Morne and rum distilleries. The Wild South Experience focuses exclusively on the raw coastal scenery, hidden natural spots and less-visited locations that most tour operators don't include.

faqs.question: What time does the tour start and finish?
faqs.answer: The tour typically departs between 7:30–8:30am from your hotel and returns in the late afternoon (around 4:00–5:00pm). Departure times can be adjusted for photographers wishing to catch early morning light. Exact times are confirmed upon booking.

mangrove-kayaking.name: Mangrove Kayaking
mangrove-kayaking.pageTitle: Mangrove Kayaking Mauritius — Guided Coastal Kayak Tours
mangrove-kayaking.pageDescription: Paddle through Mauritius's ancient mangrove forests and sheltered coastal channels on a guided kayak tour. A peaceful, immersive nature experience for all abilities. Book with MauTravel.
mangrove-kayaking.heroSubtitle: Glide silently through ancient mangrove forests and tranquil coastal channels, discovering Mauritius's extraordinary wetland ecosystems and the hidden wildlife that calls them home.
about: Mauritius's mangrove forests are among the island's most extraordinary and least-visited natural treasures. These protected coastal wetlands — where the sea meets the land in a tangle of roots, shallow channels and wildlife-rich water — offer a completely different side of the island from the resort beaches most visitors experience.

MauTravel's guided mangrove kayaking experience takes you through sheltered channels on a sit-on-top kayak, accompanied by a knowledgeable local guide who will point out the birds, fish and marine life that inhabit these fragile ecosystems. The pace is entirely gentle — this is not an adrenaline sport but a peaceful, immersive encounter with nature.

No prior kayaking experience is needed. The routes are calm and sheltered, suitable for families, couples and solo travellers of all fitness levels. A short paddling lesson is given before you set off, and the guide accompanies the group throughout to ensure everyone is comfortable and enjoying the experience at their own pace.

pricing.name: Guided Kayak Tour
pricing.description: A 2–3 hour guided paddle through Mauritius's mangrove channels with a certified local guide.

pricing.name: Private Group Tour
pricing.description: An exclusive private kayaking experience for your group — ideal for families and couples.

faqs.question: Do I need kayaking experience?
faqs.answer: Not at all. Our mangrove routes follow calm, sheltered channels that are ideal for first-time paddlers. Your guide will give a short technique lesson before you set off and will paddle alongside you throughout the experience.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for children?
faqs.answer: Yes — mangrove kayaking is one of our most family-friendly experiences. Children aged 6 and above can paddle in tandem kayaks with a parent. Life jackets are provided in all sizes. Please let us know children's ages when booking so we can prepare the right equipment.

faqs.question: What should I wear?
faqs.answer: Wear light, comfortable clothing that you don't mind getting slightly wet. A hat, sunglasses, and reef-safe sunscreen are strongly recommended. Secure footwear (water shoes or trainers) is preferred over sandals or flip-flops.

faqs.question: What wildlife might we see?
faqs.answer: Mauritius's mangrove channels are home to a variety of bird species including herons, kingfishers and egrets, as well as small fish, crabs and other marine life visible in the shallow clear water. Sightings vary by season and time of day — early morning paddles tend to be particularly rewarding for wildlife.

faqs.question: What time of day is best for kayaking?
faqs.answer: Early morning is ideal — the water is calmest, the light is beautiful, and wildlife activity is at its peak. Afternoon tours are also available and offer a different, equally enjoyable experience. We will confirm the best departure time for your group when booking.

dolphin-encounter.name: Dolphin Encounter
dolphin-encounter.pageTitle: Dolphin Encounter Mauritius — Swim with Wild Dolphins
dolphin-encounter.pageDescription: Swim with wild dolphins in Tamarin Bay, Mauritius. An unforgettable ethical wildlife encounter in the warm Indian Ocean. Book with MauTravel.
dolphin-encounter.heroSubtitle: Experience one of the most magical wildlife encounters in the Indian Ocean — swimming alongside pods of wild spinner dolphins in the warm, crystal-clear waters of Tamarin Bay.
about: Mauritius is one of very few places in the world where you can swim with wild dolphins in their natural habitat. Tamarin Bay on the west coast is home to resident pods of spinner dolphins, who gather in the bay during the early morning hours before heading out to sea.

MauTravel's dolphin encounter is an ethical, respectful wildlife experience. We work exclusively with operators who follow strict guidelines to ensure minimal disturbance to the dolphins. Guests enter the water quietly and allow the dolphins to approach naturally — there is no chasing, no touching, and no captivity.

The experience typically begins at dawn, when the dolphins are most active near shore. You'll travel by boat to find the pod, then gently slip into the water to observe and swim alongside them. It's a moment of pure magic that travellers describe as a life highlight.

pricing.name: Standard
pricing.description: Join a small shared boat for the dolphin encounter experience.

pricing.name: Family Pack
pricing.description: A dedicated family boat for a more intimate experience.

pricing.name: Private Charter
pricing.description: An exclusive private boat for your group — the ultimate dolphin experience.

faqs.question: Is it guaranteed we'll see dolphins?
faqs.answer: While dolphins are resident in Tamarin Bay and sightings are very frequent, we cannot guarantee encounters as these are wild animals. In the rare event of no dolphin sighting, we'll discuss options including a partial refund or alternative activity.

faqs.question: Can non-swimmers participate?
faqs.answer: Non-swimmers can join the boat trip and observe from above the water, but will not be able to swim with the dolphins. Life jackets are provided for all guests on board.

faqs.question: Is this suitable for children?
faqs.answer: Yes, children aged 5 and above can participate. The experience is gentle and suitable for families. Children must be accompanied by an adult in the water.

faqs.question: What time does the tour depart?
faqs.answer: The tour typically departs at sunrise (around 6:00–7:00am) when dolphins are most active near shore. Exact departure times will be confirmed when you book.

faqs.question: Are the dolphins wild or captive?
faqs.answer: The dolphins are completely wild and free. We work only with ethical operators who respect the dolphins' natural behaviour. There is no feeding, no touching, and no captivity involved.

parasailing.name: Parasailing
parasailing.pageTitle: Parasailing Mauritius — Fly Above the Indian Ocean
parasailing.pageDescription: Soar high above Mauritius's stunning lagoon on a parasailing adventure. Solo, tandem or triple options available. Book with MauTravel.
parasailing.heroSubtitle: Experience the thrill of flying high above the Indian Ocean, with breathtaking panoramic views of Mauritius's turquoise lagoon, white beaches and dramatic coastline stretching below you.
about: Parasailing in Mauritius is an exhilarating experience that combines the thrill of flying with some of the most beautiful scenery in the Indian Ocean. Tethered safely to a modern parachute and towed by a professional motorboat, you'll lift gently off the water and ascend to heights of up to 150 metres.

From your vantage point in the sky, the views are nothing short of spectacular — the varied blues and greens of the lagoon, the white ribbon of beach stretching in both directions, and the volcanic peaks of the island's interior rising behind you. It's a perspective of Mauritius that you'll never forget.

Parasailing is available in solo, tandem (two people), and triple (three people) configurations, making it ideal for couples, families, and friends. The take-off and landing both happen from the boat, so you don't even need to get wet — a great option for non-swimmers.

pricing.name: Solo
pricing.description: Take to the skies alone — full 15-minute solo flight.

pricing.name: Tandem
pricing.description: Fly together — perfect for couples and best friends.

pricing.name: Triple
pricing.description: Three up in the air at once — the most fun you'll have on holiday.

faqs.question: Do I need to be able to swim?
faqs.answer: No swimming ability is required. Take-off and landing both take place from the boat — you don't need to enter the water. Life jackets are provided for all passengers.

faqs.question: Is there a weight limit?
faqs.answer: Yes, weight and age restrictions apply for safety reasons. Please contact us with your details and we'll confirm suitability before booking.

faqs.question: Is it scary?
faqs.answer: Most guests are surprised by how smooth and peaceful parasailing is. The ascent is gradual and the flight itself is quiet and serene. Many people say it's far less frightening than they expected!

faqs.question: Can I parasail if I'm pregnant?
faqs.answer: Parasailing is not recommended for pregnant guests. Please contact us to discuss alternative activities.

faqs.question: What should I wear?
faqs.answer: Wear comfortable clothing and secure any loose items. Avoid flip-flops for safety reasons — closed shoes or bare feet are better. A change of clothes is useful as you may get splashed on the boat.

underwater-walk.name: Underwater Walk
underwater-walk.pageTitle: Underwater Walk Mauritius — Sea Walk Experience
underwater-walk.pageDescription: Walk on the seabed in Mauritius with a pressurised helmet — discover vibrant coral reefs and tropical fish. No swimming experience needed. Book with MauTravel.
underwater-walk.heroSubtitle: Walk on the ocean floor and discover Mauritius's extraordinary underwater world — no diving experience needed. Simply descend in a pressurised helmet and meet the tropical fish face-to-face.
about: The Underwater Walk — also known as a Sea Walk — is one of Mauritius's most unique and accessible water experiences. Unlike scuba diving, there's no training or swimming ability required. Guests of all ages and swimming abilities can participate.

Wearing a specially designed pressurised helmet that maintains air at a comfortable level, you descend a short ladder into the warm, clear waters and walk gently on the sandy seabed. The world around you transforms — tropical fish, sea urchins, and vibrant coral formations surround you in a living aquarium.

The descent is gradual and completely safe, accompanied by a professional underwater guide at all times. Most guests are amazed by how natural and comfortable the experience feels — many describe it as one of the highlights of their entire Mauritius holiday.

faqs.question: Do I need to know how to swim?
faqs.answer: No swimming ability is required. The underwater walk uses a pressurised helmet that keeps your head completely dry throughout the descent. You walk on the seabed rather than swimming.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for people with claustrophobia?
faqs.answer: The helmet is open at the bottom and you are always in a well-lit, open environment. However, if you have significant claustrophobia, we recommend discussing this with us before booking.

faqs.question: Is it safe for older participants?
faqs.answer: The sea walk is suitable for adults up to approximately 60 years. Guests with heart conditions, ear problems, or respiratory issues should consult their doctor before participating.

faqs.question: How deep do we go underwater?
faqs.answer: The descent is approximately 3–4 metres below the surface — deep enough to fully immerse you in the reef ecosystem while remaining safe and comfortable.

faqs.question: Will we see tropical fish?
faqs.answer: Yes — the sea walk site is located above a vibrant coral reef teeming with tropical fish, sea urchins, starfish and other marine life. Fish feeding is included to attract fish close to you.

Visitors can enjoy the scenery at a relaxed pace or add adventure experiences such as quad biking, ziplines, suspended bridges and other outdoor activities.

discoverParagraphs: Hidden within the green hills of Chamarel, Rhumerie de Chamarel offers travellers a closer look at one of Mauritius' most important traditional products: rum made directly from fresh sugarcane juice.
The estate combines agriculture, craftsmanship and modern distillation within a beautifully designed setting surrounded by sugarcane fields and tropical landscapes.

discoverParagraphs: Port Louis is the capital of Mauritius and one of the best places on the island to experience its history, culture and everyday city life.

Founded during the French colonial period in the 18th century, the city developed around its strategically important harbour and today remains the country's administrative, commercial and cultural centre.

Walk through busy streets and colourful markets, discover historic buildings and places of worship, sample Mauritian street food, explore museums and finish your visit beside the harbour at the waterfront.
Port Louis offers travellers something completely different from Mauritius' beaches and resorts: a chance to experience the energy, flavours and multicultural character of the island.

citadel-fortress.heroSubtitle: History above the heart of Port Louis. Explore a 19th-century British fortress and discover panoramic views across Mauritius' capital, harbour and surrounding mountains.
discoverParagraphs: Standing above Port Louis on a hill overlooking the capital, Fort Adelaide — commonly known as La Citadelle — is one of Mauritius' most recognisable historic fortifications.
Constructed by the British during the 19th century and completed in 1840, the fortress was designed as part of the defensive system protecting Port Louis.

Today, visitors come not only to discover its heavy basalt-stone architecture — the thick defensive walls, stone arches and old cannons that reflect the military engineering of the British colonial period — but also for the spectacular panoramic views from its elevated position.
From the Citadelle, the dense cityscape of Port Louis unfolds below, framed by mountains, the harbour and some of the capital's best-known landmarks.
It is an excellent short stop for travellers who want to combine history, photography and sightseeing during a visit to Port Louis.

discoverParagraphs: Standing beside the turquoise waters of Cap Malheureux, Notre Dame Auxiliatrice is one of the most recognisable landmarks in Mauritius.
The small Roman Catholic chapel is instantly recognisable by its vivid red roof, white exterior and spectacular coastal setting overlooking the northern islands.

The present chapel dates from the 20th century and is dedicated to the Virgin Mary. Although it attracts travellers and photographers from around the world, Notre Dame Auxiliatrice remains an active place of worship and should always be visited respectfully.

Beyond the famous postcard view, Cap Malheureux itself adds to the experience. Fishing boats, rocky shoreline, calm water and views toward Coin de Mire create one of the most distinctive coastal scenes in northern Mauritius.
It is a short stop, but one that many visitors remember long after leaving the island.

Surrounding the mountain is another side of Le Morne: turquoise lagoons, beaches, coral reefs and some of the most dramatic coastal scenery in Mauritius.

gris-gris.pageTitle: Gris Gris Mauritius | Wild South Coast Cliffs & Viewpoint Guide
gris-gris.pageDescription: Visit Gris Gris near Souillac — the raw, reef-free south coast of Mauritius where the open Indian Ocean meets black basalt cliffs. Viewpoint guide, safety advice and visitor tips.
gris-gris.heroSubtitle: The one stretch of Mauritius where no coral reef stands between the island and the open Indian Ocean.

quickInfo.label: Facilities
quickInfo.value: Free car park, benches, nearby refreshments

discoverParagraphs: Almost the whole of Mauritius sits behind a coral reef, which is why the island is ringed by calm, turquoise lagoons. Gris Gris is the exception. Here the reef simply stops, and the full weight of the Indian Ocean arrives with nothing to slow it down.

The result is a coastline that feels like a different country: dark basalt cliffs, a wind-cropped green headland and waves that break hard against the rocks below. A grassy clifftop garden with benches and shaded paths lets you take it in slowly, and on a windy day the spray carries all the way up to the viewpoint.

Local accounts differ on how the name came about — some link it to a vessel charted along this coast in the eighteenth century, others to the Creole word for a charm or talisman. Either way, it suits a place this elemental.

highlights.description: Mauritius is volcanic, and this coastline shows it plainly: dark, hard basalt cut into ledges and hollows by constant wave action.

visitingText: Gris Gris is open coastline rather than a managed attraction. There is no entrance fee, no ticket office and no fixed opening hours — but there is also no lifeguard, no barrier along much of the cliff edge and no shelter if the weather turns.

A free car park sits right at the viewpoint, and a handful of small vendors and eateries operate nearby. Most visitors spend around half an hour here, often combining it with La Roche Qui Pleure a short walk away.

faqs.question: Can you swim at Gris Gris?
faqs.answer: No. Swimming is not permitted at Gris Gris. There is no coral reef offshore to break the swell, the currents are strong and persistent, and there is no lifeguard. Gris Gris is a viewpoint rather than a bathing beach — if you want to swim on the south coast, ask your driver to suggest a lagoon-protected alternative.

faqs.question: Is there an entrance fee?
faqs.answer: No. Gris Gris is open public coastline with free access and a free car park. There is no ticket office and no official opening hours, though it is best visited in daylight.

faqs.question: How long should I allow for a visit?
faqs.answer: Around 30 to 45 minutes is enough for the viewpoint, the clifftop garden and photographs. Allow a little longer if you also want to walk across to La Roche Qui Pleure.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for older visitors or limited mobility?
faqs.answer: The main viewpoint is very close to the car park and the ground is largely level, which makes it one of the more accessible stops in the south. The paths are unpaved and uneven in places, so surfaces are not fully step-free.

faqs.question: What is the best time of day to visit?
faqs.answer: Late morning and mid-afternoon both work well. The light is strongest on the cliffs earlier and later in the day, and the site is rarely crowded at any hour.

faqs.question: Is Gris Gris worth visiting in bad weather?
faqs.answer: The sea is at its most dramatic when it is rough, which many visitors find spectacular — but that is also when it is most dangerous. Stay well back from the edge, and skip the lower path entirely when large waves are running.

la-roche-qui-pleure.pageDescription: Visit La Roche Qui Pleure near Souillac — the south coast rock formation said to resemble a weeping face. What to see, how it connects to Gris Gris, and safety advice.
la-roche-qui-pleure.heroSubtitle: A basalt outcrop on the wild south coast that, from the right angle, appears to weep as the ocean breaks over it.

quickInfo.label: Combines With
quickInfo.value: Gris Gris, a short walk away

discoverParagraphs: La Roche Qui Pleure — the rock that weeps — is a low basalt promontory a short walk east of Gris Gris along the same exposed headland. Seen from the right point on the path, its worn profile resembles a human face turned towards the sea.

The name comes from what happens when the swell arrives. Waves drive into the rock and run back off it in long streaks, so that from a distance the face appears to be streaming with tears. It is a trick of erosion and water, but a persuasive one, and it has attached itself firmly to local storytelling about loss and longing.

Souillac has a literary side too. The Mauritian poet Robert Edward Hart lived nearby at La Nef, and the village's small seafront cemetery is one of the quieter, more reflective corners of the south coast.

la-roche-qui-pleure.activitiesTitle: Things to Do at La Roche Qui Pleure

activities.name: Find the Weeping Profile
activities.description: The face only appears from certain points along the path. Walk slowly and keep looking back — the resemblance sharpens and then disappears again.

activities.name: Walk Over from Gris Gris
activities.description: A short clifftop walk links the two sites along the headland, with continuous ocean views the whole way.

activities.name: Watch the Swell Break
activities.description: Water running back off the rock is what creates the weeping effect, so the site is at its most convincing when there is a decent swell.

activities.name: Explore Souillac
activities.description: The village nearby holds the seafront cemetery where the poet Robert Edward Hart is buried, and the house at La Nef associated with him.

highlights.title: Erosion at Work
highlights.description: Every hollow and ledge in the outcrop has been cut by salt water and wind — the 'face' is simply the most photogenic result.

highlights.title: The Souillac Marine Cemetery
highlights.description: A small, weathered seafront burial ground overlooking the ocean, and the resting place of the poet Robert Edward Hart.

highlights.title: An Uncrowded Stretch
highlights.description: Most visitors stop at Gris Gris and turn back. Walking the extra few minutes usually means having this end of the headland largely to yourself.

visitingText: Like Gris Gris, this is open coastline rather than a managed attraction — free to visit, with no ticket, no gate and no fixed hours. There are no facilities at the rock itself; the nearest parking and refreshments are at the Gris Gris viewpoint.
Most visitors arrive on foot from Gris Gris and spend twenty to thirty minutes here, which is comfortably enough to find the viewing angle and take photographs.
la-roche-qui-pleure.visitingNote: Swimming and climbing down to the rocks are not advisable here. The currents along this coast are dangerous and there is no lifeguard.

The effect is strongest when the sea is rough, which is also when conditions are least safe underfoot

faqs.question: Why is it called the weeping rock?
faqs.answer: When waves break against the outcrop, the water runs back down its face in long streaks. From a distance, and from certain angles where the rock resembles a human profile, it looks as though the face is crying. The name describes that effect, and a good deal of local folklore has grown around it.

faqs.question: Can I actually see the face?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes — but only from particular points along the path, and it is more convincing to some visitors than others. Walk along slowly and look back towards the outcrop rather than straight at it.

faqs.question: How far is it from Gris Gris?
faqs.answer: It is a short walk east along the same headland, which is why almost everyone visits the two together. Allow around an hour for both sites combined.

faqs.question: Is there an entrance fee or parking?
faqs.answer: There is no entrance fee. There is no dedicated car park at the rock itself — visitors normally park at the free Gris Gris car park and walk from there.

faqs.question: Can I swim or get down to the water?
faqs.answer: No. This is the same reef-free, high-energy coastline as Gris Gris, with strong currents and no lifeguard. Stay on the clifftop paths.

faqs.question: Is it worth visiting if I've already seen Gris Gris?
faqs.answer: Yes — it is only a few minutes further on, it is usually quieter, and the rock formation itself is quite different from the wide cliff panorama at Gris Gris.

la-roche-qui-pleure.finalCtaText: The weeping rock, Gris Gris and Rochester Falls sit close together — an easy, unhurried afternoon with a private MauTravel driver.

rochester-falls.pageTitle: Rochester Falls Mauritius | Basalt Waterfall Visitor Guide
rochester-falls.pageDescription: Visit Rochester Falls near Souillac — a wide waterfall spilling over unusual squared basalt columns. How to get there, the track condition, safety advice and visitor tips.
rochester-falls.heroSubtitle: A broad curtain of water falling over rock columns squared off so neatly they look cut by hand.

quickInfo.label: Entrance
quickInfo.value: Free — informal parking fee may be asked

quickInfo.label: Access
quickInfo.value: Rough unsealed track, then a short walk

quickInfo.label: Best For
quickInfo.value: Photography, geology, a quick nature stop

quickInfo.label: Best Season
quickInfo.value: Drier months, roughly May to October

discoverParagraphs: Most waterfalls in Mauritius drop through dense green gorges. Rochester Falls does something different: it spreads sideways across a wall of basalt that has fractured into tall, squared columns, so the water falls in dozens of separate ribbons rather than a single plume.

That columnar structure is what draws people here. As the lava that formed this part of the island cooled, it contracted and cracked into regular vertical blocks — the same process that produced the famous organ-pipe formations elsewhere in the world, at a smaller and more intimate scale.

It sits in farmland just inland from Souillac, reached by a rough track through sugar cane. The falls themselves are modest in height, but the setting is green, rural and quiet, and the walk in takes only a few minutes.

whyVisit.name: Geology You Can See
whyVisit.description: The squared basalt columns behind the water are the clearest, most photogenic example of cooling-fracture rock on this side of the island.

whyVisit.name: A Wide, Unusual Fall
whyVisit.description: Rather than one narrow drop, the river spreads across the rock face and comes down in many separate strands.

whyVisit.name: Short Walk, Real Reward
whyVisit.description: Once you reach the parking area it is only a few minutes on foot — one of the most accessible waterfalls in the south.

whyVisit.name: Rural South Mauritius
whyVisit.description: The approach runs through sugar cane and smallholdings, a side of the island most visitors never see from the coast road.

visitingText: There is no official entrance fee, ticket office or set opening hours at Rochester Falls. Local attendants often watch vehicles at the informal parking area and ask for a small tip; this is customary rather than an official charge.

The access track from the main road is rough, narrow and badly rutted in places. A high-clearance vehicle is a real advantage, and after heavy rain the track can become difficult. From the parking area it is a short walk of roughly ten minutes down to the falls.
You may be approached by people offering to guide you down or to demonstrate jumping from the rocks. There is no obligation to accept, and agreeing a price beforehand avoids misunderstandings.

faqs.question: Is there an entrance fee for Rochester Falls?
faqs.answer: There is no official entrance fee. Local attendants commonly look after vehicles at the informal parking area and ask for a small tip — this is customary rather than an official charge, and the amount is up to you.

faqs.question: What is the road like?
faqs.answer: The final approach is an unsealed track through cane fields that is narrow and heavily rutted in places. A high-clearance vehicle is a real advantage, and conditions worsen after rain. On a private tour your driver will know the current state of the track.

faqs.question: Can you swim at Rochester Falls?
faqs.answer: Visitors do sometimes swim in the pool at the base, but there is no lifeguard, no depth marking and no supervision. Water depth, clarity and current change significantly with recent rainfall, so treat it with caution and never dive or jump from the rocks.

faqs.question: How long is the walk from the parking area?
faqs.answer: Roughly ten minutes on foot, on an uneven natural path. It is short but not step-free, and it can be slippery in the wet.

faqs.question: What makes the rock formation unusual?
faqs.answer: The basalt has fractured into tall, squared vertical columns with remarkably flat faces — the result of thick lava cooling and contracting. Because the water falls across this face, it splits into many separate strands instead of one plume.

faqs.question: When is the best time to visit?
faqs.answer: The drier months from roughly May to October generally give the easiest access underfoot. Water flow is heavier in the wetter season, which looks more dramatic but makes both the track and the rocks harder going.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for young children or limited mobility?
faqs.answer: The path down is uneven, unpaved and slippery in places, so it is not well suited to visitors with limited mobility. Children should be supervised closely near the water and the rock edges.

rochester-falls.finalCtaText: Rochester Falls, Gris Gris and the south coast viewpoints fit comfortably into one relaxed day with a private MauTravel driver.

alexandra-falls.pageTitle: Alexandra Falls Mauritius | Viewpoint Guide, Black River Gorges
alexandra-falls.pageDescription: Visit the Alexandra Falls viewpoint in Black River Gorges National Park — a free, easily reached panorama over forested gorges to the south coast. Access, tips and what to expect.
alexandra-falls.heroSubtitle: A short walk from the car park to one of the widest views in Mauritius — forested gorge, distant waterfall and the south coast beyond.

quickInfo.label: Location
quickInfo.value: Black River Gorges National Park, Plaine Champagne

quickInfo.label: Access
quickInfo.value: Car park within metres of the viewpoint

discoverParagraphs: Alexandra Falls is best understood as a viewpoint first and a waterfall second. The platform sits high on the southern edge of Black River Gorges National Park, looking out across a deep, densely forested valley that falls away towards the south coast — on a clear day you can follow the land all the way down to the sea.

The waterfall itself drops into the gorge off to one side. How much of it you see depends on the season and on how much the surrounding vegetation has grown: after rain it is obvious, while in a dry spell it can be modest. The panorama, on the other hand, is reliable year-round.

What makes it unusual among Mauritian viewpoints is how little effort it takes. The car park is a few metres away, the ground is largely level, and there are picnic tables under the trees — so it works for visitors who cannot manage the park's longer hiking trails.

whyVisit.name: A Big View for Almost No Effort
whyVisit.description: One of the few genuinely panoramic viewpoints in Mauritius that requires barely any walking from the car park.

whyVisit.name: Native Forest at Altitude
whyVisit.description: The gorge below holds some of the last upland native forest on the island, with the cloud-wrapped high ground of the park behind you.

whyVisit.name: Endemic Birds Overhead
whyVisit.description: The park protects species found nowhere else on earth, including the Mauritius kestrel, pink pigeon and echo parakeet.

whyVisit.name: A Natural Picnic Stop
whyVisit.description: Shaded tables near the viewpoint make this the obvious place to break a day spent crossing the south of the island.

alexandra-falls.activitiesTitle: Things to Do at Alexandra Falls

activities.name: Take in the Panorama
activities.description: The main platform looks down the length of the gorge towards the coast — the single best reason to stop here.

activities.name: Look for the Falls
activities.description: The waterfall drops into the valley to one side of the viewpoint. Visibility depends on recent rain and on seasonal growth in the vegetation.

activities.name: Watch for Endemic Birdlife

highlights.title: Upland Cloud Forest

highlights.title: Paperbark and Native Trees
highlights.description: The woodland immediately around the car park is worth a slow look in its own right, with distinctive layered bark and dense undergrowth.

visitingText: Alexandra Falls is a viewpoint within Black River Gorges National Park, and there is no entrance charge for visiting it. Parking sits immediately beside the site, and it is clearly signposted from the road that crosses the park.

It is a protected national park rather than a commercial attraction, so there is no ticket desk, no guided commentary and no shop. Most visitors stop for twenty to forty minutes, often combining it with the Black River Gorges viewpoint and Chamarel on the same drive.
alexandra-falls.visitingNote: This part of the island is considerably cooler, wetter and cloudier than the coast — bring a layer, and be prepared for the view to be obscured on a misty day.

faqs.question: Is there an entrance fee for Alexandra Falls?
faqs.answer: No. Alexandra Falls is a viewpoint inside Black River Gorges National Park and there is no charge to visit it, nor to park.

faqs.question: How much walking is involved?
faqs.answer: Very little. The viewing area is only metres from the car park and the ground is largely level, which makes this one of the most accessible viewpoints in Mauritius.

faqs.question: Will I definitely see the waterfall?
faqs.answer: Not always clearly. The falls drop into the gorge to one side of the viewpoint, and how visible they are depends on recent rainfall and on how much the surrounding vegetation has grown. The wider gorge panorama is the more reliable attraction.

faqs.question: Can I hike to the bottom of the falls?
faqs.answer: The viewpoint is exactly that — a viewpoint. It does not offer access down to the base of the waterfall. Black River Gorges National Park has a network of marked hiking trails elsewhere for visitors who want to walk in the forest.

faqs.question: What is the weather like up there?
faqs.answer: Markedly cooler, wetter and cloudier than the coast, because of the altitude. Mist can roll in quickly and obscure the view, so it is worth having a flexible plan and a light jacket.

faqs.question: What wildlife might I see?
faqs.answer: The park protects several species found nowhere else, including the Mauritius kestrel, the pink pigeon and the echo parakeet. Sightings are never guaranteed, and you are as likely to hear them as see them. Please do not feed any animals, including monkeys near the road.

belle-mare-beach.pageTitle: Belle Mare Beach Mauritius | East Coast Beach Visitor Guide
belle-mare-beach.pageDescription: A guide to Belle Mare Beach on the east coast of Mauritius — kilometres of white sand, a shallow reef-protected lagoon, filao shade and a genuinely uncrowded public beach.
belle-mare-beach.heroSubtitle: Kilometres of powder-white sand and a shallow turquoise lagoon, backed by the shade of old filao trees.

quickInfo.label: Location
quickInfo.value: Belle Mare, Flacq District — east coast

quickInfo.label: Lagoon
quickInfo.value: Shallow and calm behind a distant reef

discoverParagraphs: Belle Mare runs for several kilometres down the east coast, and it is the length that defines it. Even on a busy weekend you can walk away from the parking areas and find a stretch of sand more or less to yourself — something that is increasingly hard to do in the north or west.

The sand here is unusually fine and pale, and the lagoon in front of it is shallow, clear and calm, protected by a coral reef that sits some way offshore. That combination makes it one of the more reassuring beaches on the island for families and for anyone who prefers wading and floating to swimming out.

Behind the sand runs a belt of casuarina — filao — trees, whose thin needles cast a light, moving shade. The east coast catches the prevailing wind, which keeps the air fresher here than on the leeward side of the island and gives the water a gentle texture on all but the stillest days.

whyVisit.name: Room to Spread Out
whyVisit.description: One of the longest public beaches in Mauritius — walk a few minutes from the car park and the crowds thin out completely.

whyVisit.name: A Lagoon Built for Swimming
whyVisit.description: Shallow, clear and calm behind a distant reef, with a sandy bottom and a very gradual slope into deeper water.

whyVisit.name: Natural Shade All Day
whyVisit.description: A continuous belt of filao trees behind the sand means you are never far from somewhere cooler to sit.

whyVisit.name: The Uncommercial East
whyVisit.description: Quieter and less developed than the north and west coasts, with a slower, more local feel — especially on weekdays.

activities.name: Walk the Full Length

activities.name: Snorkel Near the Rocks

activities.name: Watch the Sunrise
activities.description: This is the east coast, so the sun comes up over the ocean — a genuine advantage over the more famous sunset beaches in the west.

activities.name: Find a Shaded Picnic Spot
activities.description: The filao belt behind the sand is the natural place to set up for a few hours out of the direct sun.

activities.name: Try the Water Sports
activities.description: Kayaks, paddleboards and other equipment are available in places along the coast, generally through hotels and independent local operators.

highlights.title: The Public Beach
highlights.description: A well-used stretch with parking, some sanitary facilities and a beach eatery — the easiest place to start if you are arriving by car.

highlights.title: The Filao Belt
highlights.description: Casuarina trees running the length of the sand, providing shade, shelter from the wind and a soft carpet of needles underfoot.

highlights.title: The Reef Line
highlights.description: Visible offshore as a line of white water. It is what keeps the lagoon calm, and it marks the limit of the safe swimming area.

visitingText: Belle Mare is a public beach with free access. There are no gates, no tickets and no opening hours, and public sections sit alongside stretches fronted by hotels — the sand itself remains open to everyone.

There is parking at the main public beach area, along with basic facilities and somewhere to buy a drink or a meal. The east coast is windier than the west, which is pleasant in the heat but does mean the lagoon surface is often lightly ruffled.
There are no lifeguards on duty along most of the beach. The lagoon is shallow and calm, but conditions can change, and swimming beyond the reef line is not advisable at any time.

faqs.question: Is Belle Mare a public beach?
faqs.answer: Yes. Belle Mare is a public beach with free access. Several hotels front sections of the coast, but the beach itself remains open to everyone, and there are public parking areas and facilities.

faqs.question: Is it safe for swimming and for children?
faqs.answer: The lagoon is shallow, calm and protected by a reef that sits well offshore, which makes it one of the gentler swimming beaches in Mauritius. However, there are no lifeguards on most of the beach, so children must be supervised and nobody should swim out past the reef line.

faqs.question: How does the east coast compare with the north and west?
faqs.answer: It is quieter, greener and less developed, and it catches more wind. That breeze keeps things comfortable in the heat, though it also means the lagoon surface is often lightly rippled rather than glassy.

faqs.question: Is there any shade?
faqs.answer: Yes — a continuous belt of casuarina (filao) trees runs behind the sand and provides natural shade for most of the day. It is one of the beach's real advantages.

faqs.question: Can I snorkel at Belle Mare?
faqs.answer: There is some snorkelling around the rockier sections and coral patches within the lagoon, best attempted on calm mornings. For richer reef life on this side of the island, Blue Bay Marine Park to the south is the stronger choice.

faqs.question: When is the best time of year to visit?
faqs.answer: Roughly May to October, during the drier and cooler season, tends to give the most reliable beach weather. The east coast can be breezy year-round.

faqs.question: Can we stop here on a private tour?
faqs.answer: Yes. Belle Mare is one of the stops on MauTravel's East Tour, and how long you spend there is entirely up to you — your itinerary can be adjusted on the day.

mahebourg-history-museum.pageTitle: National History Museum Mahébourg | Mauritius Heritage Guide
mahebourg-history-museum.pageDescription: A visitor guide to the National History Museum in Mahébourg, Mauritius — an 18th-century colonial mansion holding shipwreck relics, Battle of Grand Port history and dodo exhibits.
mahebourg-history-museum.heroSubtitle: An eighteenth-century mansion on the Grand Port coast, holding the wrecks, weapons and stories of Mauritius' contested past.

quickInfo.label: Please Note
quickInfo.value: Closed for renovation — check before travelling

discoverParagraphs: The museum occupies a French colonial country house built in the early 1770s on the banks of the La Chaux River, close to the shore of Grand Port bay. The building — long known as Château Gheude — is a listed national heritage site in its own right, with thick walls, deep verandas and the cool, shuttered rooms of pre-air-conditioning tropical architecture.

Its most significant moment came in August 1810, when the bay outside became the site of the Battle of Grand Port. The house served as a field hospital, treating wounded officers from both the French and British fleets. The battle remains the only French naval victory inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, and the museum tells its story with objects recovered from the seabed.

Beyond the battle, the collection reaches across the island's maritime and natural history: relics raised from historic wrecks, old maps and prints, colonial-era furnishings and transport, and displays devoted to the dodo and the other species Mauritius has lost.

whyVisit.description: A rare surviving eighteenth-century colonial mansion, listed as national heritage and worth the visit for its architecture alone.

whyVisit.name: Objects from the Seabed
whyVisit.description: Cannon, shot, bottles and fittings raised from ships lost in the waters just outside — history you can stand next to.

whyVisit.name: The Battle of Grand Port
whyVisit.description: The story of an 1810 naval engagement fought in the bay below, and of the house that treated the wounded from both sides.

whyVisit.name: The Dodo and What Was Lost
whyVisit.description: Displays on Mauritius' extinct and endangered endemic species — the natural-history counterpart to the island's human story.

activities.description: Cannon, grapeshot and salvaged fittings from ships lost in the 1810 battle, presented alongside the story of the engagement itself.

activities.name: Wreck Relics
activities.description: Objects recovered from historic wrecks in Mauritian waters, including material associated with the St Géran — a shipwreck woven deep into the island's literature and folklore.

activities.name: Maps, Prints and Documents
activities.description: Early charts and engravings that show how Mauritius was surveyed, settled and fought over by successive colonial powers.

activities.name: Natural History and the Dodo
activities.description: Displays devoted to the island's endemic wildlife and to the species, the dodo above all, that did not survive contact.

activities.name: Colonial Life and Transport
activities.description: Period furnishings, carriages and railway pieces that give a sense of daily life on the island in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

timeline.description: A French colonial country house rises on the banks of the La Chaux River, overlooking Grand Port bay.

timeline.title: The Battle of Grand Port
timeline.description: A French naval force defeats a British squadron in the bay outside. The house is pressed into service as a field hospital for the wounded of both fleets.

timeline.title: A Colonial Century
timeline.description: Mauritius passes to British rule later in 1810 and remains a colony until independence, a period reflected throughout the collection.

blue-bay-marine-park.pageTitle: Blue Bay Marine Park Mauritius | Snorkelling & Marine Guide
blue-bay-marine-park.pageDescription: A visitor guide to Blue Bay Marine Park near Mahébourg — a protected Ramsar wetland with clear shallow water, dozens of coral species and a thousand-year-old brain coral.
blue-bay-marine-park.heroSubtitle: A protected lagoon of exceptional clarity, sheltering dozens of coral species and one of the oldest corals in the Indian Ocean.

quickInfo.label: Location
quickInfo.value: Blue Bay, near Mahébourg — south-east coast

discoverParagraphs: Blue Bay is the most protected piece of water in Mauritius, and it shows. The bay was declared a marine national park in 1997 and recognised as a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2008, covering roughly 353 hectares of lagoon, reef, seagrass and mangrove.

That protection has paid off underwater. Surveys have recorded around 38 coral species and some 72 species of fish inside the park, along with green turtles that feed on the seagrass meadows. The lagoon is shallow, sheltered and unusually clear, which is why it is regularly named the best easy-access snorkelling site on the island.

Its most celebrated resident is a single enormous brain coral, several metres across and estimated to be over a thousand years old. Corals of this type grow only millimetres a year, which gives some sense of how long it has been sitting there — and why the rules about not touching or standing on coral matter so much here.

visitingText: The public beach at Blue Bay is free to access, with parking, shade and somewhere to buy refreshments. Swimming and snorkelling from the beach cost nothing.

Boat trips over the reef are operated by licensed local boat owners rather than by the park itself, and prices are agreed directly with them. Trips typically last around an hour and often include a snorkelling stop. Prices and departure times vary by operator and season.

Because this is a protected marine park, there are rules: no anchoring on coral, no collecting shells or coral, no fishing in the protected zone and no touching or standing on the reef. Boat operators working here are expected to follow them, and so are visitors.

conservationText: Blue Bay was declared a marine national park in 1997 and designated a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2008 — a recognition given only to sites of genuine global significance.

The park's value lies in how its habitats work together. Mangroves and seagrass meadows act as a nursery for juvenile fish, which then populate the coral reef; the reef in turn shelters the lagoon and the shoreline behind it. Damage to any one part weakens the others.

Corals are slow. The park's famous brain coral has taken over a thousand years to reach its size, growing a few millimetres annually. A single careless footstep can undo decades of that growth — which is why the no-touching rule is not a formality.

faqs.question: Is there an entrance fee for Blue Bay Marine Park?
faqs.answer: There is no charge to use the public beach or to swim and snorkel from it. Boat trips over the reef are run by licensed local operators and are paid for directly with them; prices vary, so agree them before departing.

faqs.question: Do I need to be a strong swimmer to snorkel here?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The lagoon is shallow and sheltered, which makes it one of the more forgiving snorkelling sites in Mauritius. If you are not a confident swimmer, ask your boat operator for a life jacket — they are commonly available.

faqs.question: What is a glass-bottom boat trip like?
faqs.answer: Typically around an hour, cruising slowly over the coral gardens with viewing panels set into the hull, and usually with an optional snorkelling stop. It is a good option for anyone who wants to see the reef without getting in the water.

faqs.question: Will I see turtles?
faqs.answer: Green turtles do feed on the seagrass inside the park, but sightings are never guaranteed. Boat crews know where they are most often seen. Please never chase, touch or attempt to ride marine life.

faqs.question: What is the giant brain coral?
faqs.answer: A single coral colony several metres in diameter, estimated to be more than a thousand years old — thought to be among the largest of its kind in the Indian Ocean. Because it grows only millimetres each year, it is extremely vulnerable to physical damage.

faqs.question: What should I not do in the marine park?
faqs.answer: Do not touch, stand on or break coral; do not collect shells or coral; do not fish in the protected zone; and do not feed marine life. Reef-safe sun cream, or a rash vest instead of sun cream, makes a real difference here.

faqs.question: When is the best time to snorkel?
faqs.answer: Calm mornings usually offer the clearest water, before the wind picks up. Visibility can drop after heavy rain or on windy days.

ile-aux-aigrettes.pageTitle: Île aux Aigrettes Mauritius | Nature Reserve Tour Guide
ile-aux-aigrettes.pageDescription: Visit Île aux Aigrettes, the restored coral island reserve off Mahébourg managed by the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation — pink pigeons, giant tortoises and the last dry coastal ebony forest.
ile-aux-aigrettes.heroSubtitle: A 26-hectare coral island where a lost Mauritian forest — and the species that depended on it — is being put back together.

quickInfo.label: Access
quickInfo.value: Guided tours only, booked through the MWF

discoverParagraphs: Île aux Aigrettes is a low, flat island of coralline limestone about 26 hectares in size, lying a short distance off the south-east coast near Mahébourg. It became a nature reserve in 1965, and for the past several decades it has been leased and managed by the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation.

Its significance is easy to state and hard to overstate: it holds the last meaningful remnant of Mauritius' dry coastal forest, a habitat that once fringed most of the island and has almost entirely disappeared. Restoring it has meant removing invasive plants and animals across the whole island and replanting native species by hand, year after year.

The animals came back with the forest. Pink pigeons — a species reduced to single figures in the wild by the early 1990s — were reintroduced here, along with the Mauritius olive white-eye and Telfair's skink. Aldabra giant tortoises were brought in from Seychelles in 2000 to take over the ecological job of the island's own extinct tortoises: eating fallen fruit and spreading the seeds of the native ebony.
It is, in short, one of the clearest places anywhere to see what conservation actually looks like when it works.

visitingText: Île aux Aigrettes can only be visited on a guided tour organised by the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation. There is no independent access, no landing by private boat and no unaccompanied walking — the restrictions exist to protect the reserve, and they are firmly enforced.

The standard guided eco-tour lasts roughly one and a half to two hours on the island, plus a boat crossing of about ten minutes each way from the departure point near Mahébourg. Longer and specialist options, such as photography or birdwatching visits, are offered from time to time.

Tour prices, departure times and available languages are set by the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation and change periodically. Booking ahead is strongly recommended, as places on each departure are limited.
MauTravel provides private transport to and from the departure point. The island tour itself is run by the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation and is booked and paid for separately with them.

conservationText: Before restoration began, Île aux Aigrettes had been logged for its ebony, cleared in parts, and overrun by introduced plants and animals. Very little of the original coastal forest survived.

The recovery has been slow and physical: removing invasive species across the entire island, replanting native trees by hand over many years, and only then reintroducing the animals that depend on them. Giant tortoises were part of that ecological reasoning rather than a visitor attraction — they do the seed-dispersal work that Mauritius' own extinct tortoises once did.

The results are visible on the trail. Ebony regenerating on its own, pink pigeons breeding in the wild, skinks moving through the leaf litter. It is a small island, but it is one of the strongest arguments anywhere that extinction is not always inevitable.

faqs.answer: Sightings are likely but never guaranteed — these are wild birds on a wild island. Your guide will know where they are most often seen and what to listen for.

faqs.answer: No. Touching, feeding and chasing animals are not permitted anywhere on the reserve. Observe from the distance your guide indicates and follow their instructions throughout.

faqs.question: Is it suitable for children or older visitors?
faqs.answer: The trail is gentle and mostly flat, which suits a wide range of visitors, but the ground is uneven coral limestone and much of the route is exposed to the sun. Closed shoes, a hat and water are essential.

quickInfo.value: Off Trou d'Eau Douce — east coast

quickInfo.label: Access
quickInfo.value: By boat only — shuttle or excursion

discoverParagraphs: Île aux Cerfs sits just off Trou d'Eau Douce on the east coast, inside the largest lagoon in Mauritius. That lagoon is the point: it is broad, shallow and extraordinarily clear, and the island's white sandbanks run out into it in long, pale shelves that make the water look almost artificially blue.

At around 87 hectares, it is large enough to absorb a lot of visitors and still leave quiet corners. Beach restaurants, bars and water-sports operators cluster near the main landing areas, while other stretches of shoreline stay comparatively empty — a short walk usually buys a good deal of space.

The island also holds an 18-hole championship golf course, laid out by two-time Masters champion Bernhard Langer across roughly 38 hectares of the island's interior and coastline. It is one of the most photographed courses in the Indian Ocean.
Most visitors arrive as part of an excursion — commonly a speedboat or catamaran day that also takes in the Grand River South East waterfall along the coast, with lunch on or near the island.

grse-waterfall.pageDescription: A guide to the Grand River South East (GRSE) waterfall on the east coast of Mauritius — how to see it by boat, the river estuary, resident monkeys and responsible visitor advice.
grse-waterfall.heroSubtitle: A waterfall at the mouth of the island's longest river, reached the way it is best seen — from the water.

discoverParagraphs: Grand River South East is the longest river in Mauritius, and it finishes its run in an unusual way: instead of widening quietly into the sea, it drops over a rock lip close to the estuary, so that fresh water falls almost directly into the lagoon.

That geography is exactly why it is normally visited by boat. Approaching from the water gives you the whole scene at once — the fall, the dark rock around it and the green banks closing in on either side. The land route down to the river is steep and awkward by comparison, and gives a far poorer view.

The banks along the approach are home to long-tailed macaques, which come down to the water's edge and are often the thing people remember most. They are wild animals, and feeding them is both bad for the monkeys and a reliable way to get bitten or scratched.
How impressive the falls look depends heavily on recent rainfall. After wet weather the flow is strong and loud; in a dry spell it can be considerably more modest.

The stop at the falls is usually short — long enough for the boat to approach, hold position for photographs and turn back. It is a component of a longer day rather than a destination in itself.
It is possible to reach a viewpoint over the river by land, but the path down is steep and rough and the view is much less rewarding. The boat approach is what makes this worth doing.

faqs.question: Is there an entrance fee?

faqs.question: How long do you spend at the waterfall?
